currentEvidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
currentEvidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
currentEvidence.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
currentEvidence.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

currentEvidence.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
currentEvidence.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
currentEvidence.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
currentEvidence.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development

currentEvidence.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
currentEvidence.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
currentEvidence.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
currentEvidence.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation

currentEvidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
currentEvidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
currentEvidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
currentEvidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

currentEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
currentEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
currentEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
currentEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

currentEvidence.description2: Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability.
currentEvidence.profile: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
currentEvidence.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
currentEvidence.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development

currentEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
currentEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.

currentEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

currentEvidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
currentEvidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.

currentEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
currentEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.

currentEvidence.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis

currentEvidence.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
currentEvidence.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.

currentEvidence.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
currentEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.

currentEvidence.description2: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
currentEvidence.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.

currentEvidence.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
currentEvidence.profile: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.

currentEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
currentEvidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

currentEvidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

currentEvidence.description2: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
currentEvidence.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.

currentEvidence.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
currentEvidence.profile: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.

currentEvidence.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
currentEvidence.profile: Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education. Models of radicalization and adolescent risk and protective factors lead into inclusive school climates, belonging, social-emotional learning, dialogue, media literacy and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit for an international school project, then revise the resources using feedback from intended recipients.

currentEvidence.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
currentEvidence.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
currentEvidence.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
currentEvidence.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design

currentEvidence.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
currentEvidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.

currentEvidence.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
currentEvidence.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.

currentEvidence.description2: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
currentEvidence.profile: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.

currentEvidence.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

currentEvidence.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
currentEvidence.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
